title: English idioms
examples: Teacher, what is the difference between a literal and an idiomatic phrase?
Can you give me another example of an idiom that means good luck?
Why do people use idioms in everyday conversation?

explain.say: Today we are learning about English idioms. Say that word with me. It is idiom.

items: Not the real meaning of words

explain.say: An idiom means the words together mean something different. Say the words together, but the meaning is not obvious.
For example, if I say it is raining cats and dogs. We do not mean actual animals falling. We mean it is raining very heavily.

draw.text: Raining cats and dogs = heavy rain

explain.say: One very common idiom is break a leg. When someone says this, they are not telling you to hurt yourself. They are actually wishing you good luck.
These phrases often come from old times or different cultures. They are like little pieces of history in our language. They have a long story behind them.
In real life, if you are about to go on stage for a play. Your friend might whisper break a leg to you. You know they mean you should do well.

faq.q: What does 'break a leg' actually mean?
faq.a: It is an idiom that means good luck. It is used to wish someone well before an event.
asks: What is the meaning of break a leg?
Does break a leg mean something else?

faq.a: No, not all phrases are idioms. Some phrases mean exactly what the words say, which is called literal language.
asks: How do I know if a phrase is an idiom?

faq.a: Idioms often come from old customs, historical events, or different cultures. They take time to become common.
asks: What is the source of idioms?

faq.q: Can I use idioms when I speak?
faq.a: Yes, you can use them to make your speaking more interesting. But remember to use them when you know their true meaning.
asks: Is it okay to use idioms?

faq.q: What is the difference between an idiom and slang?
faq.a: Slang changes very quickly and is often only used by a small group. Idioms are more established phrases with a fixed meaning.
asks: Is slang the same as an idiom?
What is the difference between slang and idioms?

facts: Idioms are phrases whose meaning cannot be understood from the individual words.
The phrase 'break a leg' is used to wish someone good luck.
Idioms often reflect the culture or history of the people who speak them.

quiz.say: If someone says 'spill the beans', what do they mean?
quiz.show: Spill the beans: Reveal a secret
quiz.why: This idiom means to accidentally or purposely tell a secret.

wrong.0: This is wrong because 'spilling' usually relates to liquids or small objects.
wrong.1: This is incorrect; hunger is not related to beans in this phrase.
wrong.3: This is tempting because the words suggest physical beans.

quiz.say: What is the meaning of the idiom 'piece of cake'?
quiz.why: When something is called a piece of cake, it means it required very little effort.

wrong.1: This is wrong because the idiom does not refer to actual food.
wrong.2: This is too literal and misses the figurative meaning entirely.
wrong.3: This confuses the physical nature of cake with its figurative use.

quiz.say: If a phrase means something different from its words, it is called:
quiz.why: Idioms are phrases where the combined meaning is not obvious from the separate words.

wrong.0: A simile uses 'like' or 'as' for comparison, which is different.
wrong.1: A metaphor makes a direct comparison, but idioms are fixed phrases.
wrong.2: This is the opposite of what we are learning about today.
